en.title: Pokémon VGC Star Vomits at Tournament Due to Opponent's Foul Stench
en.summary: A top Pokémon VGC competitor has sparked widespread discussion after revealing a fellow player's extreme body odor caused him to vomit during a regional championship. The incident highlights a growing concern about player hygiene at competitive gaming events.
en.body:
The competitive Pokémon circuit, known for its strategic depth and passionate fanbase, recently saw a rather pungent controversy erupt. **Donghun Youm**, a Texas-based regional champion in the Video Game Championships (VGC), took to social media to share a shocking experience at the 2026 Baltimore Regional Championships: he literally threw up due to the overwhelming stench of a nearby opponent.

Youm described the incident on Twitter/X, detailing how the smell was so overpowering that he and his friends were unable to concentrate on their matches. The situation escalated to the point where they had to inform a judge about the offensive odor. "I've had an incident at Baltimore regionals where I had to throw up due to a nearby player's stench," Youm posted. "My friends and I couldn't focus that round due to how putrid the smell was, and we even told a judge due to it. Like, c'mon man...."

## A Stinky Situation

This unfortunate event has ignited a significant conversation within the Pokémon competitive community and broader gaming circles regarding personal hygiene at large-scale events. While many players dedicate countless hours to perfecting their teams and strategies, the basic expectation of maintaining personal cleanliness seems to have been overlooked by some. The incident serves as a stark reminder that attending public events, especially those requiring close proximity and intense concentration, necessitates a baseline level of consideration for fellow attendees.

Comments on Youm's post ranged from sympathetic to outraged, with many agreeing that hygiene should be a non-negotiable aspect of attending any tournament. Some suggested that measures, such as mandatory deodorant checks or even disqualification for persistent offenders, might be necessary to ensure a comfortable environment for everyone. The debate also inevitably led to humorous comparisons with in-game Pokémon abilities that utilize smell, like the **Stench** ability, which can cause opponents to flinch.

## The Community Reacts

The fallout from Youm's revelation has been swift and widespread across social media and gaming forums. Fans and fellow competitors have shared their own less extreme, but still uncomfortable, experiences at various gaming conventions and tournaments, highlighting that this might not be an isolated issue. The sheer visceral reaction described by Youm – vomiting – has underscored the severity of the problem for many, leading to calls for greater awareness and stricter enforcement of basic etiquette.

While the Pokémon VGC is a highly respected competitive scene, this incident has unfortunately put a spotlight on a less glamorous, but equally important, aspect of player conduct. The consensus emerging is that while skill and strategy are paramount, basic respect for others, including maintaining personal hygiene, is fundamental to fostering a positive and inclusive competitive environment for all participants, from seasoned pros to casual enthusiasts.

## What's Next

As the discussion continues, it remains to be seen if tournament organizers will implement more formal guidelines or protocols regarding player hygiene. For now, the onus is on the community to self-regulate and ensure that future events are remembered for thrilling battles, not offensive odors. The next major VGC events are scheduled for later this year, with details on specific locations and dates to be announced by The Pokémon Company.

content_raw: A professional Pokémon player is going viral after begging his fellow competitors to keep up with their personal hygiene, claiming he literally threw up at an event due to someone’s stench. Texas-based Pokémon VGC regional champion Donghun Youm says he lost his lunch at the 2026 Baltimore Regional Championships thanks to a super smelly player. Youm wrote about his experience in a viral post on Twitter/X, where he begged players to “please take care of [their] personal hygiene.” Youm said someone at the competition smelled so foul that he literally threw up because of it, and his friends were unable to concentrate on their own matches due to the putrid stench. “I've had an incident at Baltimore regionals where I had to throw up due to a nearby player's stench,” he said. “My friends and I couldn't focus that round due to how putrid the smell was, and we even told a judge due to it. Like, c'mon man....” Youm’s post has kicked off a heated discourse about players’ hygiene at competitions, as well as no end of jokes and memes about certain Pokémon attacks that rely on smell to deal damage or inflict adverse status effects. (The ability ‘Stench’ was most popular, as it has a 10% chance of making your opponent flinch when hit by a damaging move.) Please take care of your personal hygiene. This is far from the first time the subject of hygiene has come up regarding in-person gaming events; in June, a card shop in Oregon suspended its Yu-Gi-Oh tournaments after receiving bad reviews and multiple complaints of smelly patrons. The shop pointed to Konami’s own tournament guidelines, which stipulate that everyone at a Yu-Gi-Oh competition, not just players, must be “clean and wear clean clothing,” or risk being “penalized.” Pokémon boasts similar rules; the official Play! Pokemon Tournament Rules Handbook includes a section regarding hygiene, which reads, “Individuals are also required to maintain a socially acceptable level of hygiene during the event. Depending on the attire or level of hygiene, the Tournament Organizer may allow for a tournament participant to change or update their personal hygiene and attire and return to the venue. "If a participant refuses to comply with tournament staff’s requests, this is grounds for removal from the tournament and venue, and the participant must relinquish their badge to tournament staff."
